heroLead: West Union is the county seat of one of the most heavily drilled counties in the state, and the courthouse here holds the deed record for nearly every mineral interest that's changed hands in Doddridge County's Marcellus and Utica boom.
intro: Doddridge County has been at the center of West Virginia's Marcellus and Utica development since the early days of the horizontal drilling era, with operators building out dense multi-well pads across the county for well over a decade. West Union sits at the middle of that activity, which means a mineral interest here is rarely a purely legacy question — it's frequently tied to a producing or recently drilled spacing unit.

Before we quote anything, we pull the Doddridge County record to trace the chain of title on your specific tract, confirm whether it's under an active lease, and check whether it's already included in a unit that's producing.

sections.heading: West Union Sits at the Center of the Marcellus Core
paragraphs: Doddridge County's geology put it at the heart of the play from the start — thick, productive Marcellus shale overlain by additional Utica and Point Pleasant potential at depth, which has made it one of the more consistently active counties in the state for over a decade of horizontal development.

That activity level is exactly why title work matters so much here. A tract that's part of an active unit is worth substantially more to a buyer than one that isn't, and confirming which situation applies to your interest is the first real step.

sections.heading: Reading a Doddridge County Deed Book
paragraphs: The mineral chain under a West Union tract often runs back through several generations of deeds, wills, and, in some cases, older tax sale records from long before drilling made the county's minerals worth much on their own. We read that full chain rather than stopping at the most recent deed, because gaps or ambiguities further back can affect what a current owner is actually entitled to sell.
This is slower work than a title search in a county with less production history, but it's necessary to make a clean offer.

sections.heading: Flat-Rate Leases That Predate the Boom
paragraphs: Some Doddridge County tracts are still bound by leases signed decades before horizontal drilling arrived, written as flat-rate agreements that pay a fixed sum with no relationship to actual production. Once a well began producing under a spacing unit covering one of these tracts, West Virginia law generally required the lease to convert to at least a 1/8 royalty.

We've found cases where that conversion never happened correctly, and the owner has been collecting a decades-old flat fee while wells nearby produce actively. That's one of the first things we check on a West Union file.

sections.heading: Heirship Fragmentation in a Core County
paragraphs: Because Doddridge County's minerals have been valuable for so long, families here have had more opportunities to split, sell partial shares, and pass fractional interests down through multiple generations than in counties where the mineral estate only recently became relevant. It's routine to find a single tract with a dozen or more heirs holding undivided fractions, some of them unaware they own anything at all.
We identify those owners through the county record and make individual offers, so no single heir needs to coordinate with the rest of the family to sell their share.

faqs.question: Is my mineral interest near West Union part of an active spacing unit?
faqs.answer: We check the Doddridge County record along with relevant permit and unit filings to confirm whether your tract is in a producing or permitted unit before we make an offer.

faqs.question: My family's lease is decades old and flat-rate. Should it have converted to a royalty by now?
faqs.answer: If a well is producing under a spacing unit that includes your tract, West Virginia's statutory 1/8 royalty floor generally applies, and the lease should have converted. We check this against the actual well and unit record.

faqs.question: I inherited a small fractional share and don't know how big it is. Can you help figure that out?
faqs.answer: Yes, that's part of the title work we do before making an offer, tracing your specific fraction through the deed and estate record.

faqs.question: Why does title research take longer in a county like Doddridge?
faqs.answer: Long production history means more deeds, leases, and estate filings to review to confirm a clean chain, but it also usually means more accurate information about what's actually producing under your tract.
